elements.text: Captain ceased right rudder input needed for directional control
Airplane encountered strong and gusty crosswind exceeding captain's training/experience
ATC system did not require or facilitate dissemination of key wind information to controllers and pilots
Inadequate crosswind training in airline industry due to deficient simulator wind gust modeling
Mountain wave conditions resulted in strong westerly winds and localized gusts up to 45 knots
Captain's use of tiller and full right control wheel resulted from acute stress and perceived lack of control
Captain's initiation of rejected takeoff was delayed by occupation with ineffective nosewheel steering tiller and control wheel input
ATC local controller did not provide information about most adverse crosswind conditions on ribbon display
Captain was not adequately prepared to respond to heading changes due to simulator training not replicating ground-level gusts
Boeing did not adequately consider dynamic handling qualities in strong/gusty crosswinds when developing guidelines
Pilots and crew were properly certificated and qualified
No evidence of medical, behavioral, toxicological, or fatigue conditions affecting pilots
Airplane was properly certificated, equipped, and maintained
No evidence of preaccident failure of powerplants, structures, or systems
Flight attendants acted appropriately during emergency evacuation
Emergency response and firefighting activities were effective
Decision to proceed with takeoff was reasonable given available wind information
Difference in wind reports likely due to timing, sensor placement, and local wind field variations
Had captain reapplied rudder, airplane would not have departed runway (counterfactual/survival factor)
Sufficient wind information would allow more informed runway selection (recommendation context)
LLWAS letter to airmen might have helped pilots request additional info (recommendation context)
Reported winds did not exceed airline maximum crosswind guidance
Had pilots received most adverse wind info, they likely would have delayed departure (counterfactual)
Noise abatement procedures did not affect runway assignment
ATC runway selection policy does not clearly account for crosswind components
Operational flight data could help FAA develop strategies (recommendation)
Seat design did not meet crashworthiness requirements (survival factor)
Flight attendant jumpseat failure due to metal fatigue (survival factor)
Adhesive fastening method in galley was inadequate (survival factor)
